tips.title: Something is fixed, something changes
tips.body: That is the whole form in six words. Usually the **structure and the harmony** stay put while the surface changes, which is why a variation lasts the same number of bars as the theme. Find what is fixed and the variations stop sounding like separate pieces.

tips.title: Say which element is varied
tips.body: "It is varied" earns nothing. **The melody is ornamented**, **the note values are halved**, **it moves to the tonic minor**, **a countermelody is added** — each of those names an element and a technique, and each one can be credited.

tips.title: Count the bars to find the joins
tips.body: Variations are almost always the **same length as the theme**. Count the theme once and you know exactly where every later variation begins, which makes it far easier to hear what has changed at each join.

tips.title: Tonic minor is not relative minor
tips.body: Moving from C major to **C minor** keeps the tonic and changes the mode; moving to **A minor** keeps the key signature and changes the tonic. Variations use both, they sound quite different, and the words are not interchangeable.

steps.title: One tune, played many ways
steps.body:
**Theme and variations** is one of the structures the Classical period favoured, alongside sonata form, rondo, and minuet and trio. It works like this.

> A **theme** is stated plainly. Then it is played again, repeatedly, with **something changed each time** and **something else held fixed**.

The fixed part is what makes it a form rather than a sequence of unrelated pieces. Usually two things stay put:

- **The phrase structure.** If the theme is 16 bars long with a cadence in the middle, each variation is normally 16 bars long with a cadence in the same place.
- **The harmony.** The chords underneath usually stay much the same, even when the tune on top has vanished.

That is why you can still follow a variation whose surface is unrecognisable: your ear is holding on to the shape and the chords, not to the notes.

**The arithmetic is worth doing once.** A theme of 16 bars with 6 variations is **112 bars** of music, because the theme is played too. Multiply by the number of variations and you lose the theme itself, which is the commonest slip in a question about this form.

**Variations are labelled** in scores and programmes as the theme, then Var. 1, Var. 2 and so on — sometimes written **A, A¹, A², A³**, which shows the idea neatly: the same letter every time, marked to say it has been altered.

props.title: A theme of 16 bars with 6 variations

visuals.alt: A table showing a sixteen-bar theme followed by six variations of the same length, with a running total of bars

props.centre: What holds a set of variations together

boxes.title: The phrase structure
boxes.body: Each variation is normally the same length as the theme, with its cadences in the same places.

boxes.title: The harmony
boxes.body: The chords underneath usually stay much the same, even when the tune has disappeared entirely.

boxes.title: The key centre
boxes.body: Most variations stay in the home key. One or two may move, and those stand out because of it.

boxes.title: Your memory of the theme
boxes.body: Everything depends on the theme being stated plainly first, so the listener has something to hold.

visuals.alt: Four boxes explaining what stays fixed across a set of variations

check.prompt: A theme is 16 bars long and is followed by 6 variations, each the same length. How many bars of music is that altogether?
check.solution: There are 6 variations **plus the theme itself**, so 7 sections of 16 bars: 16 times 7 is **112**. Multiplying by 6 instead gives 96 and quietly loses the theme, which is the usual mistake.

markScheme.description: 16 times 7 = 112

steps.title: Varying the melody and the rhythm
steps.body:
The two easiest elements to vary are the two most obvious ones.

**Melody: ornamentation.** The theme is kept but decorated — trills, turns, grace notes, passing notes filling in the gaps between its notes. The skeleton is still there underneath and a listener can usually pick it out. This is the commonest opening variation, because it lets the composer move without letting go.

**Melody: it can also be broken up.** The theme's notes are turned into arpeggios or scales that pass through them, so the tune is implied by the outline rather than played.

**Rhythm: diminution.** Every note value is **halved**. A crotchet becomes a quaver, a minim becomes a crotchet. Twice as many notes now fit in a bar, so the variation sounds **twice as busy** — but the tempo has not changed and the variation is still 16 bars long. That is the point people miss: diminution changes the notes, not the speed of the beat.

**Rhythm: augmentation.** The opposite. Every note value is **doubled**, so the theme becomes broad and slow while the pulse stays where it was.

**Rhythm: dotting.** A pair of even notes becomes a **dotted** pair, long then short. A dot adds half again, so a dotted crotchet plus a quaver fills exactly the same time as two crotchets — the bar still adds up, and only the character has changed.

**Rhythm: triplets.** Three notes in the time of two. Again the bar is unchanged; the feel is not.

Notice what all four rhythmic techniques have in common: **the bar still holds the same amount**. A variation that changed the total would fall out of step with the harmony underneath it.

rows: trills, turns and passing notes added
even pairs become long then short
three notes in the time of two
a rolling feel against the beat
props.title: Varying the melody and the rhythm

visuals.alt: A table of five ways to vary the melody or rhythm of a theme, what each does to the notes and how each sounds

visuals.problem: A theme moves in crotchets. In the third variation it moves in quavers at the same tempo. Name the technique, and say what does and does not change.

steps.text: Each crotchet has become a quaver, which is half its value.
steps.note: Halving every note value is diminution. Doubling them would be augmentation.

steps.text: Where 4 crotchets filled a semibreve, 8 quavers do.
steps.note: So twice as many notes now fit in the same bar, and the variation sounds twice as busy.

steps.text: The tempo has not changed and neither has the bar length.
steps.note: The beat is exactly where it was. Only the notes inside each beat have multiplied.

steps.text: So the variation is still 16 bars and still fits the same harmony.
steps.note: That is the whole reason the technique works: the surface changes and the frame does not.

check.prompt: A variation halves every note value of the theme while the tempo stays exactly the same. What is the technique, and what is the effect?
options: Augmentation: the theme is stretched out and sounds slower
Accelerando: the beat gradually gets faster through the variation
Diminution: twice as many notes a bar, so it sounds busier
Syncopation: the notes fall between the beats instead of on them
check.solution: Halving the note values is **diminution**. Twice as many notes fit in each bar, so the surface is twice as busy — but the tempo and the bar lengths are untouched, which is why the variation still fits the theme’s harmony. Augmentation is the opposite; an accelerando changes the tempo itself; syncopation moves stresses off the beat.

markScheme.description: diminution, busier at the same tempo

steps.title: Varying the tonality and the harmony
steps.body:
Changing the key is the most dramatic thing a variation can do, and there are two quite different ways to do it.

**The tonic minor.** A theme in **C major** is played in **C minor**. The tonic stays; the mode darkens. Three of the seven notes change, and the effect is immediate — the same tune, suddenly shadowed. Most sets of variations have one of these and it is usually the emotional centre of the movement.

**The relative minor.** A theme in **C major** moves to **A minor** — or in G major to E minor, or in B flat major to G minor. Here the **key signature does not change at all**, because a major key and its relative minor contain exactly the same notes. What moves is the tonic, so the music sounds shifted rather than darkened.

> Tonic minor: same tonic, different notes. Relative minor: same notes, different tonic. They are not interchangeable, and an exam will happily ask which one you heard.

**Reharmonisation.** The tune stays and the chords underneath it change. A phrase that was harmonised with simple triads comes back with chromatic chords, or with a chord substituted at the cadence, so a familiar melody arrives somewhere unexpected.

**Changing the cadences.** A phrase that closed with a **perfect** cadence may close with an **interrupted** one instead — V to VI rather than V to I — which sets up an ending and then refuses it.

**Adding chromaticism.** Notes from outside the key, sliding by semitones, used to colour a harmony that was plain in the theme.

One caution. The harmony is usually the thing that **stays**, so a variation that changes it is making a point. Notice when it happens and say so.

props.title: The two minors, from three major keys

visuals.alt: A table giving the tonic minor and the relative minor for three major keys

boxes.title: Tonic minor
boxes.body: C major to C minor. The tonic stays, three notes change, and the key signature changes with them.

boxes.title: Relative minor
boxes.body: C major to A minor. Every note is the same and the key signature does not change; the tonic moves.

boxes.title: How they sound
boxes.body: A tonic minor darkens the same music. A relative minor shifts the centre of gravity sideways.

boxes.title: Why it matters
boxes.body: An exam question can ask which one a variation used, and the two words are not interchangeable.

visuals.alt: Four boxes distinguishing the tonic minor from the relative minor

check.prompt: A theme in C major returns in A minor. What has changed?
options: The tonic has moved; the notes and key signature are the same
The mode has changed; three of the seven notes are different
Both the tonic and every note of the scale have changed
Nothing has changed except the speed at which it is played
check.solution: A major key and its **relative minor** share every note and therefore the same key signature — C major and A minor both have none. What moves is the **tonic**. A change to the **tonic minor**, C major to C minor, would be the other option: same tonic, three notes different.

markScheme.description: the tonic moved; the notes stayed the same

steps.title: Varying the texture, the forces and the speed
steps.body:
The remaining elements are the ones that change the **sound** of a variation rather than its notes.

**Texture: adding a countermelody.** A new melodic line is written against the theme. The theme is still there, but now something else is competing for attention, so the texture thickens from melody-and-accompaniment towards **polyphony**.

**Texture: canon or imitation.** The theme is set against itself, one part entering after another. This is the most obviously clever variation a composer can write, and it is usually placed late in a set.

**Texture: stripping it back.** The opposite, and often more effective. One line alone, or two, where there were four. A **monophonic** variation in the middle of a busy set is a real event.

**Sonority: a different instrument.** In an orchestral set, the theme moves from strings to woodwind to brass. In a piano set, it moves between the hands or into a different **register** — the same notes an octave or two higher sound thinner and brighter, lower they sound heavier.

**Tempo.** A variation marked slower or faster than the theme. Notice that this is a different thing from diminution: **tempo** changes the speed of the beat, **diminution** changes the notes inside it. A set often has one genuinely slow variation, and it usually goes with the tonic minor.

**Metre.** A theme in three beats a bar reappearing in four, or in compound time. This is the most disorientating change of all, because the phrase lengths have to be rebuilt to keep the structure.

**Dynamics and articulation.** The same variation played **staccato** rather than **legato** is a different piece of music, and the specification lists articulation as an element in its own right.

props.title: Twelve ways to vary a theme, and what each one changes

visuals.alt: A table listing twelve variation techniques with the musical element each one alters

visuals.problem: How would you describe a variation where the theme appears in the cellos an octave lower, with a new flute melody above it, marked staccato?

steps.text: Sonority: the theme has moved to the cellos.
steps.note: Naming the instrument is worth more than saying the sound has changed.

steps.text: Register: it is an octave lower than the theme.
steps.note: The same notes lower sound heavier and darker. Register and sonority are related but separate observations.

steps.text: Texture: a new flute melody has been added above it.
steps.note: That is a countermelody, and it pushes the texture towards polyphony.

steps.text: Articulation: the marking is staccato rather than legato.
steps.note: Articulation is an element in its own right, and the specification defines it as how far a note is separated from the next.

steps.text: Four elements named, four techniques named.
steps.note: That is a full answer. "It is varied by changing the instruments" is a quarter of one.

check.prompt: A variation adds a completely new melodic line above the theme, which continues underneath unchanged. What is the new line called, and what does it do to the texture?
options: An ostinato, which makes the texture monophonic
A pedal, which makes the texture homophonic
A countermelody, which pushes the texture towards polyphony
A sequence, which leaves the texture unchanged
check.solution: A new melody written against an existing one is a **countermelody**, and with two independent lines competing for attention the texture moves towards **polyphony**. An ostinato repeats at the same pitch; a pedal is a held note; a sequence is repetition at a different pitch.

markScheme.description: a countermelody, moving the texture towards polyphony

steps.title: The ground bass: the same idea upside down
steps.body:
Theme and variations fixes the **tune** and varies what happens around it. There is a Baroque form that does exactly the opposite.

**A ground bass** is a short phrase in the bass that repeats over and over while everything above it changes. The specification calls it a type of **ostinato**, "especially in some Baroque pieces, notably by Purcell". It goes by other names too: **basso ostinato**, and in dance forms the **passacaglia** and **chaconne**.

Put the two side by side and the family resemblance is obvious.

| | Theme and variations | Ground bass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is fixed | the tune, and the harmony under it | the bass line |
| What varies | everything around the tune | everything above the bass |
| Where it sits | mostly Classical | mostly Baroque |
| Typical length | 16 bars or so | three or four bars |

The shorter unit is why a ground bass feels relentless where variations feel sectional: the pattern comes round every few seconds rather than every few phrases.

**Your set work does this.** Purcell's *Music for a While* is built on a ground bass three bars long, entirely in quavers and arpeggio based, repeating while the voice above it changes continuously. Because the ground ends on **chord V**, each repetition is unresolved until the next one starts, so the music never comes to rest.

That is worth noticing as a technique in itself. A theme-and-variations movement usually closes each variation properly, so the listener gets a breath between them. A ground bass refuses to, which is exactly why it suits a lament.

props.title: Three forms built on something repeating

visuals.alt: A table comparing theme and variations, ground bass and passacaglia by what stays fixed and what varies in each

check.prompt: Name the Baroque form in which a short bass phrase repeats throughout while the parts above it change, used by Purcell in Music for a While.
check.solution: A **ground bass**, or basso ostinato. It is theme and variations turned upside down: instead of fixing the tune and varying its surroundings, it fixes the bass and varies everything above. Purcell was regarded as a master of it.

markScheme.description: ground bass

steps.title: A set of variations, worked
steps.body:
Here is a set described as an exam might present it. Work through it naming the element and the technique for each variation.

**The theme.** 16 bars in C major, four crotchets in a bar, at a moderate tempo. A simple tune in the right hand of a piano over plain chords in the left. Two eight-bar phrases, the first closing on chord V and the second on chord I.

**Variation 1.** The same length and the same chords. The tune is still recognisable but is now decorated with trills, turns and passing notes filling the gaps between its original notes.

**Variation 2.** The same length and the same chords. The right hand now moves in quavers where the theme moved in crotchets, at the same tempo.

**Variation 3.** The same length. Now in C minor. The tempo is slower and the dynamic is quiet throughout.

**Variation 4.** The same length and back in C major. The theme appears in the left hand, two octaves below where it started, with a new melody above it in the right.

**Variation 5.** The same length. The right hand states the theme and the left hand follows one bar later with the same notes, while the right continues.

**Variation 6.** The same length and the same chords, but now in three crotchets a bar instead of four, marked fast and loud.

rows: ornamentation: trills, turns and passing notes
the tonic minor, and a slower tempo
the theme moved down two octaves, with a countermelody above
canon: the left hand imitates the right a bar later
four crotchets a bar becomes three, fast and loud
props.title: The six variations, named

visuals.alt: A table naming the element varied and the technique used in each of the six variations in the worked example

visuals.problem: Why is Variation 3 the centre of the movement?

steps.text: It is the only one that changes the mode.
steps.note: C major to C minor is the tonic minor: the tonic stays and three notes of the scale change.

steps.text: It is also the only one that slows down.
steps.note: A change of tempo is different from diminution: here the beat itself is slower, not the notes inside it.

steps.text: And it is quiet throughout, where the others are not.
steps.note: Three elements changing at once — tonality, tempo and dynamics — after five variations that changed one or two.

steps.text: So it is the point of greatest contrast with the theme.
steps.note: Composers usually place the minor variation near the middle for exactly this reason, and the movement is shaped around it.

check.prompt: In that set, Variation 5 has the left hand playing the theme a bar after the right hand, while the right continues. What is that?
options: A countermelody
Augmentation
Canon, a form of imitation
Reharmonisation
check.solution: One part stating an idea and another taking up **the same idea** a bar later while the first continues is **imitation**, and strict imitation of a whole line is a **canon**. A countermelody would be a *different* new line; augmentation doubles note values; reharmonisation changes the chords underneath.

markScheme.description: canon, or strict imitation

steps.title: Why a composer chooses this form
steps.body:
Every form solves a problem. This one solves a particular problem very neatly, and saying so is what lifts an answer out of the middle bands.

**The problem: variety without losing the listener.** Music that keeps repeating becomes dull; music that keeps changing becomes impossible to follow. Theme and variations gets both at once, because **the listener always knows where they are**. The phrase structure and the harmony are fixed, so however strange the surface becomes, the ear still has the frame to hold on to.

**It also shows off.** A set of variations is a display of craft — here is my tune, and here are twelve things I can do to it without breaking it. That is part of why it was so popular in the Classical period, when composers frequently performed their own music and wrote variations on tunes their audience already knew.

**It shapes easily.** A set has a natural dramatic arc available to it: start plainly, get gradually busier, place a slow minor variation near the middle for contrast, and finish with the fastest and loudest. That is the shape of the worked example above, and it is extremely common.

**And it is a good test of listening.** Which is exactly why the exam likes it. To answer a question about a variation you have to hear what has changed **and** what has not, and the second half is the harder one.

> The mark scheme rewards the element and the technique. *The note values are halved, which is diminution, so it sounds twice as busy although the tempo has not altered* is one point made properly. *It gets faster and more exciting* is not a point at all — and it is also wrong, because nothing got faster.

rows: The second variation is more complicated
The note values are halved, so twice as many notes fill each bar
It gets faster in variation two
The tempo is unchanged; diminution makes it busier, not faster
Variation three is in a minor key
Variation three is in the tonic minor, C major becoming C minor
The theme moves to the left hand two octaves lower, with a countermelody above
The left hand imitates the right a bar later: a canon
The harmony and the sixteen-bar structure are fixed throughout
props.title: The same six observations, made weakly and made well

visuals.alt: A table pairing six weak statements about a set of variations with the precise version of each

check.prompt: What does theme and variations give a composer that a set of unrelated short pieces would not?
options: The chance to write in several different keys at once
A way of making a short piece of music last much longer
Variety while the listener always knows where they are
An excuse not to write more than one good melody
check.solution: The fixed phrase structure and harmony mean the listener can follow the music however far the surface travels. That is the trade the form makes, and it is the thing to say in a question about why a composer would use it. Length and key changes are consequences, not the point.

markScheme.description: variety without the listener losing their place

steps.title: Going deeper: hearing what has not changed
steps.body:
Most students describe what changed. The ones who reach the top band describe what **stayed**, because that is the harder listening and it is what makes the form work.

**Three things to listen for underneath.**

**The phrase structure.** Count the theme once. If it is two eight-bar phrases with a cadence in the middle, listen for that cadence in the middle of every variation. It is almost always still there, however unrecognisable the surface. A variation that *breaks* the structure is doing something unusual and worth remarking on.

**The harmony.** The chords are usually the deepest fixed layer. A variation whose melody has dissolved into scales and arpeggios is still moving through the theme's chords, which is exactly why it still sounds like the theme.

**The bass line.** Often nearly unchanged, and often the easiest thing to follow when the top has gone wild.

**Then say what changed, precisely.** Name the element, then the technique, then the effect:

> *In the second variation the note values are halved — diminution — so twice as many notes fill each bar and the surface sounds busier, although the tempo and the sixteen-bar structure are exactly as they were.*

That sentence names the element, names the technique, gives the effect, and shows what was held constant. It is one point, and it earns on both halves of a mark scheme.

**Two traps.**

**Diminution is not acceleration.** The beat does not move. Students write "it gets faster" and lose the mark, because it is the wrong description of the right observation.

**Tonic minor is not relative minor.** C major to C minor keeps the tonic; C major to A minor keeps the key signature. Both appear in variation sets and they do not sound alike.

boxes.title: The phrase length
boxes.body: Count the theme once and you know where every join is. Almost always identical.

boxes.title: The harmony
boxes.body: The deepest fixed layer. It is why a variation still sounds like the theme when the tune has gone.

boxes.title: The bass
boxes.body: Often nearly unchanged, and the easiest thing to follow when the top is unrecognisable.

boxes.title: Then the change
boxes.body: Name the element, the technique and the effect. Three things, in that order, every time.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on what to listen for in a set of variations, three fixed and one changing

check.prompt: Which sentence would earn most in a question about a variation?
options: The second variation is much more complicated and exciting than the theme
It gets faster in this variation, which builds the energy of the movement
The composer varies the theme here by changing how the music is played
The note values are halved, so it sounds busier although the tempo is unchanged
check.solution: It names the technique, gives the effect, and says what was held constant. The second and fourth name nothing at all; the third names something that did not happen — diminution changes the note values and leaves the beat exactly where it was, so "it gets faster" is the wrong description of a right observation.

markScheme.description: the option naming the technique, the effect and what stayed fixed

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- A **theme** is stated plainly, then repeated with **something changed** and **something held fixed**.
- What is usually fixed: the **phrase structure** and the **harmony**. That is what lets a listener follow.
- A 16-bar theme with 6 variations is **112 bars**, because the theme is played too.
- **Melody**: ornamentation, or breaking the tune into scales and arpeggios.
- **Rhythm**: **diminution** halves the note values, **augmentation** doubles them. Neither changes the tempo. Also dotted rhythms and triplets.
- **Tonality**: the **tonic minor** keeps the tonic and darkens the mode; the **relative minor** keeps the key signature and moves the tonic. C major goes to C minor or to A minor, and they are different.
- **Harmony**: reharmonisation, changed cadences, added chromaticism.
- **Texture**: a **countermelody**, **canon** or imitation, or stripping back to one line.
- **Sonority**: a different instrument, or a different register.
- **Tempo, metre, dynamics and articulation** can all be varied too.
- A **ground bass** is the same idea upside down: fix the bass, vary everything above. Purcell's *Music for a While* is a set work built that way.
- Always name the **element**, the **technique** and the **effect**.

rows: The tune decorated with trills and turns
Twice as many notes, same tempo
Half as many notes, same tempo
A new tune above the theme
The theme chasing itself a bar later
The theme an octave or two lower
A short bass phrase repeating throughout
props.title: Straight from what you hear to the word for it

visuals.alt: A table pairing eight things heard in a set of variations with the technical term for each

check.prompt: In a set of variations, what is normally held fixed?
options: The instrumentation and the dynamics
The tempo and the note values
Nothing at all: every element changes
The phrase structure and the harmony
check.solution: The **phrase structure** and the **harmony** are the usual fixed layers, which is why each variation is the same length as the theme and still fits underneath it. Instrumentation, dynamics, tempo and note values are all things composers vary — indeed they are the main tools of the form.

markScheme.description: the phrase structure and the harmony

questions.prompt: In a set of variations, what is normally held fixed while everything else changes?
options: The instruments and the dynamic level
The phrase structure and the harmony
The note values and the tempo
Nothing: every element is varied in turn
questions.solution: The **phrase structure** and the **harmony**. That is what makes the form work: however far the surface travels, the listener still has the length of the phrases and the chords underneath to hold on to. Instruments, dynamics, note values and tempo are among the things composers vary.

markScheme.description: the phrase structure and the harmony

questions.prompt: A variation keeps the theme but decorates it with trills, turns and passing notes. Give the term for this.
questions.solution: **Ornamentation**: the process of elaborating or decorating musical material, particularly a melody, including conventional ornaments such as trills and turns. It is the commonest opening variation because the theme stays audible underneath the decoration.

markScheme.description: ornamentation

questions.prompt: A theme in C major is played again in C minor. What has changed?
options: The mode: the tonic is the same and three notes are different
The tonic: the notes are the same and the key signature is unchanged
The tempo: minor keys are conventionally played more slowly
Nothing audible: C major and C minor use the same seven notes
questions.solution: C major to C minor is the **tonic minor**: the tonic stays put and the **mode** changes, which alters three of the seven notes and the key signature with them. Keeping the notes and moving the tonic would be the **relative** minor, A minor.

markScheme.description: the mode changed; the tonic stayed

questions.prompt: A theme is 16 bars long and is followed by 6 variations of the same length. How many bars long is the whole movement?
questions.solution: The theme is played as well as the 6 variations, so there are 7 sections of 16 bars: **112** bars. Multiplying 16 by 6 gives 96 and loses the theme.

questions.prompt: Every note value in a variation is halved while the tempo stays the same. What is the technique called?
options: Diminution
Augmentation
Accelerando
Syncopation
questions.solution: **Diminution**. Twice as many notes now fit in each bar, so the variation sounds busier — but the beat has not moved and the variation is still the theme's length, which is why it still fits the same harmony. Augmentation doubles the values instead.

markScheme.description: diminution

questions.prompt: A new melodic line is written above the theme, which continues underneath. Give the term for the new line.
questions.solution: A **countermelody**: a second melodic line written against the theme. With two independent melodies competing for attention the texture moves towards **polyphony**, which is itself worth saying.

markScheme.description: countermelody

accepted: a new melodic line against the theme

questions.prompt: A theme in G major returns in E minor, and the key signature does not change. Which relationship is that?
options: The tonic minor
The dominant minor
The subdominant major
The relative minor
questions.solution: E minor is the **relative minor** of G major: the two share every note and therefore the same key signature, which is exactly why nothing on the page changes. The **tonic** minor would be G minor, which keeps the tonic and alters three notes.

markScheme.description: the relative minor

questions.prompt: One part states the theme and another follows a bar later with the same notes while the first continues. What is that called?
options: Countermelody
Sequence
Ostinato
Canon
questions.solution: Strict imitation of a whole line, one part following another, is a **canon**. A countermelody would be a *different* new line; a sequence is repetition at a different pitch; an ostinato is a short pattern repeating at the same pitch.

markScheme.description: canon

questions.prompt: Name the Baroque form in which a short bass phrase repeats throughout while the parts above it change.
questions.solution: A **ground bass**, which the specification calls a repeating phrase in the bass, a type of ostinato, especially Baroque and notably by Purcell. It is theme and variations the other way up: the bass is fixed and everything above it varies.

markScheme.description: ground bass

questions.prompt: Why does a variation almost always last the same number of bars as the theme?
options: So it still fits the theme’s harmony and phrase structure
Because composers were required to write it that way
So that the whole movement divides into equal minutes
Because a longer variation would need a different key
questions.solution: The harmony and the phrase structure are the fixed layers of the form. A variation of a different length would fall out of step with both, and the listener would lose the thread that makes a set of variations one piece rather than several.

markScheme.description: so it still fits the harmony and phrase structure

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you should take them when a question asks you to describe a variation.
items: Check what has stayed the same: the length, the harmony, the bass
Decide which musical element has been changed
Name the technique used to change it
Say what effect the change has on the music
Say how the variation contributes to the shape of the whole set
questions.solution: What stayed comes first, because it is the harder listening and because it tells you what kind of change you are looking for. Then the element, which narrows the field, then the technique, which names it. The effect follows the technique — an appraising point is only credited where an observation supports it. The place in the whole set comes last, because it needs everything else established first.

markScheme.description: what stayed fixed before what changed
the element and technique before the effect
the contribution to the whole set last

questions.prompt: A student writes that a variation with halved note values "gets faster". What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing is wrong: halving the note values does speed the music up
The note values were doubled, not halved, so it gets slower
The tempo is unchanged; there are simply more notes in each bar
Tempo cannot be described at all in a variations question
questions.solution: **Diminution** changes the notes, not the beat. The pulse stays exactly where it was and the variation is still the theme’s length; what changes is that twice as many notes fit inside each beat, so the **surface** is busier. "It gets faster" is the wrong description of a correct observation, and it loses the mark.

markScheme.description: the tempo is unchanged; the notes are shorter

questions.prompt: A set of variations places its one slow, quiet, tonic minor variation near the middle. Why?
options: It is the greatest contrast with the theme, so it shapes the whole set
A minor variation is technically easier to play than a major one
Convention requires every variation set to contain one minor variation
The performer needs a rest in the middle of a long movement
questions.solution: Changing mode, tempo and dynamic at once makes it the furthest point from the theme, and putting it in the middle gives the movement an arch: plain, increasingly busy, a point of maximum contrast, then a fast loud finish. That is a judgement about the **shape of the whole**, which is what the top band asks for.

markScheme.description: it is the point of greatest contrast and gives the set its shape

questions.prompt: A theme moves in crotchets in four-four time. In one variation every note value is halved, at the same tempo. How many notes now fill a bar that previously held 4 crotchets?
questions.solution: Halving a crotchet gives a quaver, and 8 of those fill the same bar that held 4 crotchets. So **8** notes. The tempo has not changed at all: this is diminution, not acceleration.

markScheme.description: 4 crotchets becomes 8 quavers

questions.prompt:
A set of variations for piano is played several times.

**The theme.** 16 bars in G major, four crotchets in a bar, at a moderate tempo. A simple melody in the right hand over plain chords in the left, in two eight-bar phrases, the first closing on chord V and the second on chord I.

**Variation 1.** 16 bars, same chords. The melody is still recognisable but is filled out with trills, turns and passing notes between its original pitches.

**Variation 2.** 16 bars, same chords, same tempo. The right hand now moves in quavers where the theme moved in crotchets.

**Variation 3.** 16 bars. The music is now in G minor, the tempo is slower and the dynamic is quiet throughout.

**Variation 4.** 16 bars, back in G major. The theme is in the left hand, two octaves below its original register, with a new melody above it.

**Variation 5.** 16 bars. The right hand states the theme and the left hand follows a bar later with the same notes while the right continues.

Describe how the theme is varied in each of the five variations, naming the element changed and the technique used.
questions.solution:
**What stays fixed.** Every variation is **16 bars** long, and all but the third keep the theme's chords. That is the frame, and it is why the set holds together: the listener always knows where they are in the phrase, however unrecognisable the surface becomes.

**Variation 1 varies the melody.** The tune is still there but is filled out with trills, turns and passing notes between its original pitches — **ornamentation**. It is the gentlest possible first move: the theme has only just been stated and the listener can still hear it under the decoration.

**Variation 2 varies the rhythm.** The right hand moves in quavers where the theme moved in crotchets, at the same tempo. That is **diminution**: every note value halved, so 8 notes now fill a bar that held 4. The variation sounds twice as busy, but the **beat has not moved** and the variation is still 16 bars, which is why it still fits the same chords. Writing "it gets faster" would be the wrong description of this.

**Variation 3 varies the tonality, the tempo and the dynamics at once.** G major becomes **G minor**, which is the **tonic minor**: the tonic stays and three of the seven notes change. Crucially this is *not* the relative minor — that would be E minor and would not change the key signature. On top of the change of mode the tempo is slower and the dynamic quiet throughout, so three elements move together. After two variations that each changed one thing, this is the point of greatest contrast with the theme, and it is almost certainly the emotional centre of the set.

**Variation 4 varies sonority, register and texture.** The theme moves to the **left hand, two octaves lower**, so the same notes sound heavier and darker — a change of **register**. Above it a new melodic line appears: a **countermelody**, which pushes the texture from melody-and-accompaniment towards **polyphony**, since two independent lines are now competing for attention.

**Variation 5 varies the texture again, and more strictly.** The left hand follows the right a bar later **with the same notes** while the right continues: that is **imitation**, and strict imitation of a whole line is a **canon**. It is the most obviously skilful variation of the five, and composers usually place such a variation late in a set for exactly that reason.

**The shape of the set.** Taken together the five make an arch. The first two change one element each and stay close to the theme; the third is the furthest point from it, changing three at once; the fourth and fifth rebuild in the major, growing in contrapuntal interest towards the canon. Nothing at all has changed in the phrase structure from beginning to end.

questions.prompt:
A set of orchestral variations is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the leading melodic line only.

**The theme.** 16 bars in B flat major, three crotchets in a bar. Strings alone, playing a melody over chords, quietly.

**Variation 1.** 16 bars, same chords. A solo oboe takes the melody over sustained strings; every note value is doubled, so the melody moves at half its former rate although the beat is unchanged.

**Variation 2.** 16 bars, same chords. The full orchestra, loud. The melody is in the brass in octaves, in dotted rhythms where the theme was even.

**Variation 3.** 16 bars. Now in G minor, with no change of key signature. A solo cello plays the melody; the strings accompany, pizzicato.

**Variation 4.** 16 bars, back in B flat major, now in four crotchets a bar instead of three. The melody passes from flutes to clarinets to horns, four bars each, over a timpani roll.

Describe how the theme is varied in each of the four variations, and explain what has been held fixed across the set.
questions.solution:
**What is fixed.** All four variations are **16 bars** long, and the first two keep the theme's chords. The phrase structure survives even the change of metre in the fourth, which is the hardest case, since moving from three crotchets a bar to four means the bar lines fall in different places and the phrasing has to be rebuilt to come out at the same length.

**Variation 1 varies sonority and rhythm.** The melody moves from the strings as a body to a **solo oboe** over sustained strings, so the texture thins to one clear line with an accompaniment. Every note value is **doubled**, which is **augmentation**: the melody now moves at half its former rate although the **beat is unchanged**. The effect is broad and unhurried rather than slow, because the pulse underneath is exactly where it was — augmentation is not a change of tempo, and saying so is the mark of an accurate answer.

**Variation 2 varies sonority, dynamics and rhythm.** The full orchestra plays loudly and the melody is in the **brass in octaves**, which is the loudest and most penetrating way an orchestra can state a tune and carries no harmony of its own. The even notes of the theme have become **dotted rhythms** — a long dotted note paired with a short one — which sharpens the character towards a march or a fanfare. Against Variation 1 this is the maximum possible contrast in forces and dynamic.

**Variation 3 varies tonality and sonority.** It moves to **G minor**, and the detail that the key signature does **not** change is what identifies it: B flat major and G minor contain exactly the same notes, so this is the **relative minor** and not the tonic minor. A move to the tonic minor would be B flat minor and would require a new key signature. The tonic has shifted rather than the mode darkening, so the effect is of the music leaning sideways rather than clouding over. The sonority thins again to a **solo cello**, and the accompanying strings play **pizzicato** — plucked rather than bowed — which removes all sustain from the accompaniment and leaves the cello line exposed.

**Variation 4 varies metre and sonority.** Three crotchets a bar becomes **four**, which is the most disorientating change available, since the stresses fall in different places and the phrase lengths must be recalculated. The melody then passes from **flutes to clarinets to horns**, four bars each, over a **timpani roll**, so the colour changes three times within the variation itself while the material stays the same.

**Overall.** The set is shaped by contrast in forces: solo oboe, then full orchestra, then solo cello, then a passage handed around the sections. Underneath all of it the 16-bar structure never moves, which is what makes four very different pieces of music into one movement.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between theme and variations and a ground bass?
options: They are two names for exactly the same musical form
A ground bass is a theme and variations played backwards
They are unrelated: one is a form and the other is a texture
Both fix one element and vary the rest, but a different element
questions.solution: Theme and variations fixes the **tune** and its harmony and varies what surrounds them. A **ground bass** fixes the **bass line** and varies everything above it. The principle — something fixed, something changing — is the same; the element chosen is not. Purcell’s *Music for a While* is a set work built the second way.

markScheme.description: the same principle, applied to a different fixed element

questions.prompt: Which observation about a set of variations would be hardest to make, and therefore earns most?
options: That the third variation is in a minor key rather than a major one
That the last variation is the loudest and fastest of the set
That the harmony and phrase structure are unchanged throughout
That the theme is stated plainly before any variation begins
questions.solution: Hearing what has **not** changed is much harder than hearing what has, and it is the observation the form depends on. A change of mode, a loud finish and a plainly stated theme are all obvious on a first hearing; the survival of the harmony underneath an unrecognisable surface is not.

markScheme.description: that the harmony and phrase structure are unchanged

questions.prompt: Explain why a composer might choose theme and variations rather than writing several separate short pieces, and explain what a listener is holding on to when a variation no longer resembles the theme.
questions.solution:
**The problem the form solves.** Music that repeats becomes dull; music that keeps changing becomes impossible to follow. Theme and variations gets both at once, and that is the whole reason to choose it over a handful of separate short pieces. Separate pieces give variety but no continuity — nothing connects the third to the first. A set of variations gives just as much variety and the continuity as well.

**What the listener holds on to.** Two layers stay fixed. The **phrase structure**: each variation is normally the theme's exact length, with its cadences in the same places, so a listener who has counted the theme once knows where every join and every half-close will fall. And the **harmony**: the chords underneath usually survive intact, so a variation whose melody has dissolved into scales and arpeggios is still moving through the theme's chord progression. Very often the **bass line** is nearly unchanged too, and it is frequently the easiest thing to follow when the top of the texture has become unrecognisable.

That is why a variation can be unrecognisable and still not be lost. The ear is not tracking the notes of the tune; it is tracking the shape and the chords, and those are still there.

**The variety available.** Once the frame is fixed, almost everything else is free. The **melody** can be ornamented with trills, turns and passing notes, or broken into arpeggios that only imply it. The **rhythm** can be halved — **diminution** — so the surface sounds twice as busy without the beat moving at all, or doubled — **augmentation** — so it becomes broad. The **tonality** can move to the **tonic minor**, keeping the tonic and darkening the mode, or to the **relative minor**, keeping every note and moving the tonic. The **texture** can gain a **countermelody**, or be set in **canon** against itself, or be stripped back to a single line. The **sonority**, **register**, **tempo**, **metre**, **dynamics** and **articulation** can all be changed. That is a very large number of genuinely different pieces of music from one tune.

**The shape of a whole set.** Because the units are equal, a composer can shape the sequence deliberately: begin plainly, grow busier, place a slow quiet variation in the **tonic minor** near the middle as the point of greatest contrast, then build back to the fastest and loudest at the end. The listener experiences that as a single arch rather than as a list.

**The same idea inverted.** A **ground bass** makes the opposite choice: it fixes the **bass** and varies everything above it. Purcell's *Music for a While* does this, over a three-bar ground. Because that unit is so much shorter than a sixteen-bar theme, the effect is relentless rather than sectional, and because the ground ends on chord V each repetition is unresolved until the next begins. So the two forms share a principle and produce almost opposite experiences — which is itself evidence that the principle, and not the surface, is what matters.

examTechnique.body:
**The form in one sentence.** A theme is stated plainly, then played again repeatedly with something changed each time, while something else is held fixed.

**Name the element and the technique.** Every variation changes something nameable: melody, rhythm, tonality, harmony, texture, tempo, metre, sonority or dynamics. Say which, and say how.

**Count the theme.** Variations are normally its exact length, so counting once tells you where every join is.

**Listen for what stays.** Usually the harmony and the phrase structure. That is what lets a listener follow the theme even when the surface is unrecognisable.

**Use the right words for rhythm.** Halving the note values is **diminution** and doubling them is **augmentation**. Both keep the theme and change its speed on the page rather than the tempo.

**Know the two minors.** **Tonic minor** keeps the tonic and darkens the mode. **Relative minor** keeps the key signature and moves the tonic. They sound different and the exam distinguishes them.

**The ground bass is the same idea upside down.** Theme and variations fixes the tune and varies what surrounds it; a ground bass fixes the bass and varies what sits above. Purcell's *Music for a While* is a set work built the second way.

**Say why a composer varies.** Variety without losing the listener: the form lets a piece stay recognisable while going somewhere.
examinerErrors: Writing "the theme is varied" without saying which element changed.
Confusing the tonic minor with the relative minor.
Calling a change of tempo a diminution, when diminution is a change of note values.
Missing that the harmony has stayed the same, which is usually the thing holding the movement together.
Describing a variation as a new theme, when its phrase structure is identical.
Counting the theme as one of the variations, so the arithmetic comes out one short.
Saying a variation is "more complicated" rather than naming ornamentation, added parts or shorter note values.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer says what is fixed before it says what changes, because the fixed part is what makes the form work. It names the element and the technique in the same breath — the note values are halved, which is diminution, so the variation sounds twice as busy without the tempo altering — and it distinguishes a change of mode from a change of key. It hears the phrase structure surviving under an unrecognisable surface, and it can explain why a composer would choose the form at all: it buys variety without ever losing the listener.
